DOI: [10.7554/eLife.95802.3.sa2](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.95802.3.sa2)

Summary:

This work describes a statistical framework that combines functional linear mixed modeling with joint 95% confidence intervals, which improves statistical power and provides less conservative and more robust statistical inferences than in previous studies. Pointwise linear regression analysis has been used extensively to analyze time series signals from a wide range of neuroscience recording techniques, with recent studies applying them to photometry data. The novelty of this study lies in (1) the introduction of joint 95% confidence intervals for statistical testing of functional mixed models with nested random-effects, and (2) providing an open-source R package implementing this framework. This study also highlights how summary statistics as opposed to trial-by-trial analysis can obscure or even change the direction of statistical results by reanalyzing two other studies.

Strengths:

The open-source package in R using a similar syntax as lme4 package for the implementation of this framework, the high fitting speed and the low memory footprint, even in complex models, enhance the accessibility and usage by other researchers.

The reanalysis of two studies using summary statistics on photometry data (Jeong et al., 2022; Coddington et al., 2023) highlights how trial-by-trial analysis at each time-point on the trial can reveal information obscured by averaging across trials. Furthermore, this work also exemplifies how session and subject variability can lead to different conclusions when not considered.

This study also showcases the statistical robustness of FLMM by comparing this method to fitting pointwise linear mixed models and performing t-test and Benjamini-Hochberg correction as performed by Lee et al. (2019).

Summary:

Loewinger et al. extend a previously described framework (Cui et al., 2021) to provide new methods for statistical analysis of fiber photometry data. To demonstrate its utility, they reanalyze datasets from two recent fiber photometry studies into mesolimbic dopamine. Then, through simulation, they demonstrate the superiority of their approach compared to other common methods.

Strengths:

The statistical framework described provides a powerful way to analyze photometry data and potentially other similar signals. The provided package makes this methodology easy to implement and the extensively worked examples of reanalysis provide a useful guide to others on how to correctly specify models.

Modeling the entire trial (function regression) removes the need to choose appropriate summary statistics, removing the opportunity to introduce bias, for example in searching for optimal windows in which to calculate the AUC. This is demonstrated in the re-analysis of Jeong et al., 2022, in which the AUC measures presented masked important details about how the photometry signal was changing. There is an appropriate level of discussion of the interpretation of the reanalyzed data that highlights the pitfalls of other methods and the usefulness of their methods.

These methods should have wide applicability to those who use photometry or similar methods. The development of this excellent open-source software is a great service to the wider neuroscience community.

results.result: Common fiber photometry analysis strategies reduce the detection of effects by condensing within-trial signals into summary measures and discarding trial-level information through trial-averaging. These approaches may dilute important patterns related to individual animal differences and signal evolution across trials.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4, C16, C18-C19, C43-C45 collectively establish that current photometry analysis methods have significant limitations. The characterization is based on field knowledge and is well-supported by the literature review and examples provided (C21-C26). The authors demonstrate these limitations empirically through Figure 1 and subsequent reanalyses.

results.result: Existing photometry-specific analysis methods have critical limitations: encoding models lack time-point-specific inference and reduced power from single-animal fitting; permutation methods are restricted to two-condition comparisons; standard GLMs/correlations require trial-averaging; and the Lee et al. 2019 method is overly conservative and sampling-rate dependent.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C42, C46-C47 provide a comprehensive critique of existing methods with appropriate citations. The limitations are logically argued based on statistical principles (e.g., C35, C37, C39-C42). The authors later empirically validate the Lee et al. critique through direct comparison (C130-C132).

results.result: The proposed FLMM framework enables hypothesis testing at every trial time-point using trial-level signals without averaging, compares timing and magnitude across conditions while accounting for between-animal differences, and produces joint 95% confidence intervals that improve effect detection over standard multiple comparison corrections.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C10, C48-C54 describe the core capabilities of FLMM. These are well-supported by the methodological development (C55-C79), empirical demonstrations on real data (C94-C129), and simulation validation (C133-C141). The framework successfully addresses the limitations identified in existing methods.

results.result: FLMM combines linear mixed models and functional regression to extract information both across and within trials, modeling covariates at trial, session, and animal levels while using functional random-effects to capture between-animal variability. Joint confidence intervals exploit autocorrelation to enable interpretation across time intervals rather than single time-points.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C73 describe the technical foundation of FLMM with appropriate citations (C60, C69). The methodological approach is clearly explained and builds on established statistical methods. The joint CI construction is a key innovation that is validated in simulations (C134-C141).

results.result: The authors extended the FLMM framework to enable joint 95% CIs for general random-effects specifications, including nested models. This extension substantially improved model fits in the neuroscience experiments analyzed and addresses a gap in existing methodological implementations.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C76, C142-C144 describe a genuine methodological contribution. The extension is properly motivated by the gap in existing methods (C74, C143) and validated through improved model fits (C75, C144). The derivation is based on established statistical approaches (C76) and detailed in Appendix 3.

results.result: FLMM reanalysis of the Jeong et al. 2022 IRI-dopamine association revealed two distinct temporal components: a rapid component peaking before lick-onset (possibly reflecting motivation/reward detection) and a slower component after lick-onset (possibly tracking consumption). Standard AUC analysis averaged across these components, obscuring their distinct dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claims C11, C94-C104 demonstrate FLMM's ability to reveal effects obscured by summary measures. The finding is supported by Figure 4 showing the IRI-DA association throughout the time window [-0.5, 1.5] sec (C97). The interpretation of two components (C98-C102) is reasonable given the temporal dynamics, though speculative elements are appropriately qualified (C100, C102).

results.result: FLMM reanalysis revealed that the Reward Number-dopamine association is negative within-session but positive across-sessions, contradicting the original Jeong et al. 2022 finding of a positive correlation. This discrepancy represents Simpson's paradox caused by pooling data without accounting for hierarchical structure. DA increases across sessions during reward anticipation but decreases within-session during consumption.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C119 identify a critical reanalysis finding with major implications. The Simpson's paradox explanation (C113-C114) is well-supported by Figure 5A showing opposing within-session and across-session slopes. The FLMM properly accounts for nested structure (C110), and the temporal dynamics (C115-C118) provide mechanistic insight. This directly contradicts the original paper's interpretation regarding RPE vs. ANCCR models.

results.result: FLMM detected a significant reduction in mean dopamine during the falling portion of the cue-elicited response (1-2.5 sec after cue-onset) when delay was lengthened from 3 to 9 seconds, an effect that was obscured in the original Jeong et al. 2022 AUC analysis because opposing effects in different time windows canceled out.
results.evaluation: Claims C124-C129 demonstrate FLMM's ability to detect subtle temporal effects missed by AUC analysis. The finding is supported by Figure 6H showing the specific time window of the effect. The explanation for why AUC missed this effect (C127) is logical - the significant reduction in interval (2) was diluted by the non-significant increase in interval (1). This exemplifies the value of time-point-specific analysis.

results.result: Simulation experiments based on realistic photometry data characteristics demonstrated that FLMM achieves nominal joint and pointwise 95% CI coverage across sample sizes, substantially improves statistical power over standard methods (LMM, t-test, permutation), and commits Type I errors at nominal levels, indicating it is not overly susceptible to trial-level noise.
results.evaluation: Claims C133-C141, C173-C176 provide rigorous validation of FLMM's statistical properties. The simulations incorporated realistic data characteristics (C133) and compared against appropriate alternatives. Figure 7 shows FLMM achieves ~95% joint coverage (C134) while permutation methods do not (C135), and FLMM has superior power (C138). The nominal Type I error rate (C175) addresses concerns about analyzing trial-level data.

results.result: FLMM's proportion of significant time-points is stable across sampling rates, while the Lee et al. 2019 approach shows inconsistent and often low (conservative) proportions across sampling rates, demonstrating the advantage of modeling signals as functions and exploiting temporal correlation.
results.evaluation: Claims C130-C132 provide empirical validation of the critique of the Lee et al. 2019 method (C38-C42). The comparison directly demonstrates the sampling-rate dependence problem predicted theoretically (C41). This is referenced to Appendix 2 for full details, and the interpretation (C132) logically follows from the results.

results.result: Alternative explanations for the within-session dopamine decreases include photobleaching, satiation/habituation, learning about reward-delivery mechanism cues, or elevated indicator expression. However, the ability to detect both within-session increases (to cues) and decreases (to rewards) on the same trials argues against photobleaching as the sole explanation.
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C123, C150-C157 appropriately acknowledge alternative explanations for the reanalysis findings. The photobleaching argument (C121-C123) is logical but relies on additional analyses in Appendix 4.3. Other explanations (C150-C155) are speculative and cannot be definitively ruled out. The authors appropriately qualify these as possibilities rather than conclusions. Personal communication with original authors (C123) adds credibility but is not peer-reviewed evidence.

results.result: The reanalysis findings have implications for competing models (RPE vs. ANCCR) of dopamine's role in reward learning, but adjudicating between these models is beyond the scope of the current work. The authors suggest that modeling trial-level dopamine as a vector or function may improve theories for its role in reward learning.
results.evaluation: Claims C147-C149, C158-C160, C166-C169 appropriately acknowledge the theoretical implications while recognizing the limitations of the current work. The authors correctly note that model predictions depend on specific implementations (C149, C167) and that their findings suggest future work is needed (C166). The suggestion about functional modeling (C168-C169) is reasonable speculation supported by citations.

results.result: The Jeong et al. 2022 dataset exhibits common photometry data characteristics including nested longitudinal structure, high within-animal correlations across sessions and trials, between-animal variability in covariate-signal associations, and missing data with varying sample sizes. FLMM can model these characteristics through functional random-effects and accommodates missing data.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C93 characterize the dataset and justify FLMM's design choices. The data characteristics are demonstrated in Figure 3 (C84-C85, C89, C93). The capabilities of FLMM to handle these characteristics (C86-C87, C90-C92) are logical consequences of the mixed-effects framework and are validated through successful model fitting.

results.result: Reanalysis of a second study (Coddington et al. 2023) measuring calcium dynamics demonstrated FLMM's applicability to different photometry sensors and additional capabilities including modeling how signal dynamics early in training predict later behavior and estimating covariate interactions across trial time-points and sessions.
results.evaluation: Claims C170-C172 demonstrate generalizability of FLMM beyond dopamine sensors. The reanalysis is detailed in Appendix 6 and shows additional capabilities. This strengthens the case for FLMM as a general framework, though the appendix location suggests these are supporting rather than primary results.

results.result: The authors provide the fastFMM package (first to provide joint CIs for functional mixed models with nested random-effects), which is fast, maintains low memory footprint, can fit generalized models with count distributions, and allows non-linear covariate-signal relationships using splines or basis functions.
results.evaluation: Claims C196-C200, C202, C207 describe the software implementation. The claim of being 'first' (C196) is qualified with 'to our knowledge' and supported by the literature review (C74, C143). Performance claims (C200) are supported by a timing example in the Methods. The capabilities (C202, C207) are standard extensions of the framework.

results.result: FLMM may reduce biases from summary statistics by preserving temporal resolution to disentangle neural sub-populations, makes model misspecification easier to identify through visual inspection, and may improve reproducibility by incorporating pre-processing steps into the model framework with explicit uncertainty quantification.
results.evaluation: Claims C177-C194 describe potential benefits of FLMM for scientific practice. The bias reduction argument (C177-C180) is logical given photometry measures aggregate activity. The model misspecification claim (C181) is supported by the authors' experience. The reproducibility argument (C183-C194) is well-reasoned - incorporating pre-processing into the model makes assumptions explicit and quantifies uncertainty. These are appropriately framed as potential benefits rather than proven advantages.

results.result: FLMM is applicable to a wide range of experimental settings and may extend to other techniques like electrophysiology and calcium imaging. The method can be extended to model time-varying covariates, enabling analysis of simultaneously recorded signals from different brain regions and trials with variable lengths, though flexibility-interpretability tradeoffs must be considered.
results.evaluation: Claims C195, C201, C203-C208 describe the scope and potential extensions of FLMM. The broad applicability (C195) is supported by the range of analyses demonstrated. Extensions to other techniques (C201) and time-varying covariates (C203-C205) are reasonable given the framework's generality. The caution about complexity (C208) is appropriate for a method designed for inference.

results.result: Photometry signals from a Pavlovian reward learning task (Coddington et al. 2023) exhibit considerable heterogeneity across animals, conditions within-animal, trials within-session, and sessions. Averaging across trials can obscure behavior-signal associations, and AUC summarization can fail to distinguish signals with different dynamics but similar summary values.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C26 are supported by Figure 1 showing data from Coddington et al. 2023. The heterogeneity is visually apparent in panels A-D. The inferences about averaging and AUC (C25-C26) logically follow from the observed variability. This motivates the need for FLMM but is not a primary result of the current work.

results.result: FLMM is well-suited to assess dopamine backpropagation questions by testing signal timing evolution within and across sessions. Reanalysis results align with Jeong et al. 2022 but contrast with Amo et al. 2022. Initial exploration suggests between-animal variability in backpropagation timing may require explicit modeling.
results.evaluation: Claims C161-C165 discuss the backpropagation hypothesis with reference to Appendix 4.4. The argument for FLMM's suitability (C161) is logical. However, the 'initial exploration' (C164) and recommendation for future work (C165) suggest this analysis is incomplete. The contrast with Amo et al. (C163) is noted but not resolved. This appears to be preliminary work requiring further investigation.

results.result: Linear mixed models can analyze trial-level summary measures without trial-averaging but still require condensing signals into scalars. Functional regression can test associations at each time-point but most methods require trial-averaging. Both approaches have complementary strengths and limitations.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C59 provide background on the component methods underlying FLMM. These are accurate characterizations of LMM and functional regression based on established statistical knowledge. The limitations identified (C57, C59) motivate the need to combine these approaches in FLMM (C60). This is pedagogical background rather than a novel result.

results.result: Fiber photometry quantifies bulk fluorescence from biosensors with high specificity, has increased in popularity nearly exponentially since development, and enables chronic implantation for longitudinal experiments. Common analysis procedures were adapted from other fields rather than designed specifically for photometry.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C15, C17, C20 provide accurate background on fiber photometry with appropriate citations. The exponential growth claim (C15) is supported by Appendix 1-figure 1. The historical development (C17) and chronic implantation capability (C20) are well-established facts. This is standard background material.

results.result: Research on statistical methods for fiber photometry is necessary given the widespread use of the technique and variability of analysis procedures across labs.
results.evaluation: Claim C209 is a concluding statement supported by the entire paper. The widespread use is documented (C15), the variability in analysis approaches is demonstrated through the literature review (C16-C42), and the need for better methods is established through the limitations identified and improvements demonstrated. This is a well-supported conclusion.

results.result: Fiber photometry is a popular technique for measuring neural activity in vivo with high specificity, but there is little consensus on analysis strategies, and common approaches have grown organically from other fields.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly acknowledge the popularity and utility of fiber photometry, with one stating 'Fiber photometry has become a very popular tool in recording neuronal activity in freely behaving animals.' The characterization of the field and lack of standardized analysis is accepted without challenge across all reviews.

results.result: Common photometry analysis strategies condense within-trial signals into summary measures and discard trial-level information by averaging across trials, which can reduce the detection of effects and dilute important patterns in the data.
results.evaluation: All reviewers explicitly agree with this characterization. One reviewer states 'most of the data analyses confine to simple measurements of averaged activity and by doing so, erase valuable information encoded in the data.' Another notes that the study 'highlights how summary statistics as opposed to trial-by-trial analysis can obscure or even change the direction of statistical results.'

results.result: The proposed FLMM framework enables hypothesis testing at every trial time-point using trial-level signals without averaging, compares timing and magnitude of signals across conditions while accounting for between-animal differences, and produces interpretable plots with joint 95% confidence intervals.
results.evaluation: Reviewers consistently affirm the framework's capabilities. One states 'The framework the authors present is solid and well explained.' Another notes 'The statistical framework described provides a powerful way to analyze photometry data' and that 'Modeling the entire trial (function regression) removes the need to choose appropriate summary statistics.'

results.result: The FLMM methodology yields joint 95% confidence intervals that exploit signal autocorrelation, account for inspecting effects across the entire trial, and improve detection of event-related signal changes over common multiple comparisons correction strategies. The authors extended existing methods to enable joint CIs for general random-effects specifications.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly recognize this as a key methodological contribution. One reviewer states the novelty lies in 'the introduction of joint 95% confidence intervals for statistical testing of functional mixed models with nested random-effects.' The technical advancement is accepted without challenge.

results.result: FLMM reanalysis of Jeong et al., 2022 data revealed significant effects obscured by standard approaches, including identification of two dopamine components with distinct temporal dynamics in response to reward delivery (one rising rapidly before lick-onset possibly reflecting motivation/movement/reward detection, and another beginning after lick-onset possibly tracking sucrose consumption).
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm these findings. One states 'the reanalysis of two studies using summary statistics on photometry data (Jeong et al., 2022; Coddington et al., 2023) highlights how trial-by-trial analysis at each time-point on the trial can reveal information obscured by averaging across trials.' Another notes 'the re-analysis of Jeong et al., 2022, in which the AUC measures presented masked important details about how the photometry signal was changing.'

results.result: FLMM reanalysis found that the Reward Number–DA association is negative within-session (contrary to the positive correlation reported by Jeong et al., 2022), with the discrepancy arising from pooling trials across sessions without considering hierarchical structure (Simpson's paradox). DA increases across sessions in response to reward anticipation but decreases within-session during reward consumption.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly acknowledge this finding. One states 'this work also exemplifies how session and subject variability can lead to different conclusions when not considered.' The identification of Simpson's paradox and the opposing within- vs. between-session effects are accepted as valid findings from the reanalysis.

results.result: FLMM estimated that mean DA was significantly lower in the latter parts of the cue-elicited DA response (approximately 1–2.5 sec after cue-onset) on long- compared to short-delay trials, an effect that may have been occluded in the original analysis because the AUC averaged over opposing effects. This demonstrates FLMM's ability to detect subtle effects difficult to identify by eye.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this as a demonstration of FLMM's capabilities. One reviewer notes 'Modeling the entire trial (function regression) removes the need to choose appropriate summary statistics, removing the opportunity to introduce bias, for example in searching for optimal windows in which to calculate the AUC.' The delay-change finding is treated as evidence of the method's sensitivity.

results.result: In simulation experiments incorporating realistic photometry data characteristics, FLMM achieved joint 95% CI coverage at roughly nominal levels, improved statistical power over common analysis approaches (LMM, t-test, permutation methods), achieved nominal pointwise coverage, and committed type I errors at roughly nominal levels, demonstrating it is not overly susceptible to trial-level noise or spurious correlations.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm the simulation results. One states 'through simulation, they demonstrate the superiority of their approach compared to other common methods.' Another notes 'The evidence supporting the benefits of the presented functional mixed-effect modeling analysis as opposed to (1) summary statistics and (2) other pointwise regression models is convincing with a thorough comparison with other methods and datasets.'

results.result: Photometry signals exhibit considerable heterogeneity across animals, conditions, trials within-session, and sessions. The Jeong et al., 2022 dataset exhibited nested longitudinal structure with high within-animal correlations across sessions and trials, and between-animal variability in covariate-signal associations.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these data characteristics as motivation for the method. One states the work demonstrates 'trial-by-trial temporal analysis, taking also into account variability within the dataset.' The characterization of photometry data complexity is not challenged.

results.result: FLMM combines benefits of linear mixed models and functional regression to extract information both across- and within-trials, estimates effects of covariates varying between trial/session/animal, adjusts for between-animal differences through functional random-effects, and can accommodate missing data and different sample sizes.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm these capabilities. One states 'The authors' use of linear mixed methods, allows for the estimation of random effects, which are an important consideration given the repeated-measures design of most photometry studies.' The technical capabilities are accepted without challenge.

results.result: Comparison with the Lee et al., 2019 approach showed that FLMM's proportion of significant time-points is stable across sampling rates, while the Lee et al. approach is inconsistent and often highly conservative. This illustrates advantages of modeling trial signals as functions and using information across the entire trial.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly acknowledge this comparison. One states 'This study also showcases the statistical robustness of FLMM by comparing this method to fitting pointwise linear mixed models and performing t-test and Benjamini-Hochberg correction as performed by Lee et al. (2019).' The comparative advantage is accepted.

results.result: The authors extended the FLMM framework to enable parameter estimation with pointwise and joint 95% CIs for general random-effect specifications, filling a gap in previous implementations. Nested random-effects specifications substantially improved model fits in the reanalyzed experiments.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly recognize this as a technical contribution. One states the novelty lies in 'the introduction of joint 95% confidence intervals for statistical testing of functional mixed models with nested random-effects.' The methodological extension is accepted without challenge.

results.result: FLMM allows direct comparison and testing of differences in signal time-courses between conditions and can reveal significant effects that were tested but obscured by summary measure analyses, including subtle effects difficult to identify by eye.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm this capability. One states 'the reanalysis of two studies using summary statistics on photometry data (Jeong et al., 2022; Coddington et al., 2023) highlights how trial-by-trial analysis at each time-point on the trial can reveal information obscured by averaging across trials.' The demonstrated capability is accepted.

results.result: Reanalysis of a second study (Coddington et al., 2023) measuring calcium dynamics demonstrated FLMM's applicability to different photometry sensors and additional capabilities to model how signal dynamics early in training predict behavior later in training and estimate covariate interactions across trial time-points and sessions.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge the breadth of application. One states 'The evidence supporting the benefits of the presented functional mixed-effect modeling analysis as opposed to (1) summary statistics and (2) other pointwise regression models is convincing with a thorough comparison with other methods and datasets.' The second reanalysis is accepted as supporting evidence.

results.result: The authors provide an analysis guide and open source package (fastFMM), the first to provide joint CIs for functional mixed models with nested random-effects. The package is fast and maintains a low memory footprint even for complex models and large datasets.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly praise the software contribution. One states 'The open-source package in R using a similar syntax as lme4 package for the implementation of this framework, the high fitting speed and the low memory footprint, even in complex models, enhance the accessibility and usage by other researchers.' Another calls it 'a great service to the wider neuroscience community.'

results.result: Despite photometry data complexity, there are few analysis methods developed specifically for photometry. Existing methods (encoding models, Jean-Richard-Dit-Bressel et al. 2020, standard GLMs/correlations, pointwise methods) have various limitations including not testing associations at each time-point, not pooling across subjects, not adjusting for multiple comparisons, or not exploiting correlation across time-points.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this characterization of the field. One states 'there are currently no standardized ways to analyze the data produced' and 'most of the data analyses confine to simple measurements of averaged activity.' The critique of existing methods is not challenged.

results.result: Linear mixed models can analyze trial-level summary measures preventing loss from trial-averaging but still require condensing signals into scalar measures. Functional regression can test associations at each time-point but most methods require trial averaging, discarding trial-level information.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this as background establishing the need for FLMM. The characterization of LMM and functional regression limitations is not challenged and serves as motivation for the combined approach.

results.result: The authors discuss alternative interpretations of the reanalysis findings, including that observed DA changes may be inconsistent with RPE or ANCCR models depending on specifications, and that satiation, habituation, learning about reward-delivery cues, or indicator expression changes may contribute to observed effects. Adjudicating between theoretical models is beyond the scope of the paper.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the discussion of alternative interpretations. One notes 'There is an appropriate level of discussion of the interpretation of the reanalyzed data that highlights the pitfalls of other methods and the usefulness of their methods.' The acknowledgment of interpretive limitations is not challenged.

results.result: FLMM may reduce biases from summary statistics, help disentangle signal components from different neural sub-populations, make model misspecification easier to identify, and improve reproducibility by eliminating some pre-processing steps or making their effects clearer. The method provides a systematic framework to model signal components and quantify uncertainty from modeling choices.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these potential benefits. One states 'More in depth analysis, more variables taken into account, better statistical power all lead to higher quality science.' The discussion of broader implications is not challenged.

results.result: FLMM is applicable in a wide range of experimental settings and may extend to other techniques like electrophysiology and calcium imaging. The package allows modeling of non-linear covariate-signal relationships and can be extended to model time-varying covariates. Research on statistical methods for fiber photometry is necessary given widespread use and variability of analysis procedures.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm broad applicability. One states 'This work will be of great interest to researchers using not only fiber photometry, but other time-series data such as calcium imaging or electrophysiology data.' Another notes 'These methods should have wide applicability to those who use photometry or similar methods.'

comparisons.comparison: Perfect alignment on Simpson's paradox finding (C105-C119). Both recognize the critical reanalysis revealing opposing within-session vs. across-session effects in Coddington et al. data, with OpenEval providing detailed technical explanation and peer reviewers explicitly affirming the finding's validity.

Perfect alignment on delay-change detection (C124-C129). Both agree FLMM revealed temporal effects missed by AUC analysis in Jeong et al. reanalysis, with OpenEval explaining the dilution mechanism and peer reviewers accepting this as demonstration of method sensitivity.

Perfect alignment on generalizability (C170-C172). Both agree FLMM extends beyond dopamine sensors to other recording modalities, with OpenEval noting Appendix 6 details and peer reviewers affirming broad applicability across datasets.

Perfect alignment on broader scientific benefits (C177-C194). Both accept potential advantages for bias reduction, reproducibility, and scientific practice, with OpenEval framing as potential benefits and peer reviewers affirming these lead to higher quality science.

Perfect alignment on methodological background (C55-C59). Both accept characterization of LMM and functional regression limitations as motivation for FLMM, treating this as pedagogical background establishing need for combined approach.

Strong alignment on simulation validation (C133-C141, C173-C176). Both affirm FLMM achieves proper coverage and superior power. OpenEval provides detailed technical validation while peer reviewers explicitly state simulations demonstrate superiority and provide convincing evidence.

Strong alignment on IRI-DA association findings (C11, C94-C104). Both agree FLMM reveals effects obscured by summary measures, with OpenEval noting speculative elements are appropriately qualified and peer reviewers affirming trial-by-trial analysis reveals information masked by averaging.

Strong alignment on FLMM core capabilities (C5-C10, C48-C54). Both affirm the framework's capabilities are well-supported, with OpenEval citing methodological development and empirical demonstrations, while peer reviewers state the framework is solid, well-explained, and powerful.

Strong alignment on critique of existing methods (C27-C42, C46-C47). Both accept comprehensive critique with appropriate citations, with OpenEval noting logical arguments based on statistical principles and peer reviewers affirming lack of standardization and limitations of simple measurements.

Strong alignment on joint CI contribution (C74-C76, C142-C144). Both recognize extension for nested random effects as genuine methodological contribution, with OpenEval noting validation through improved fits and peer reviewers explicitly identifying this as key novelty.

Strong alignment on limitations of current methods (C1-C4, C16, C18-C19, C43-C45). Both agree current photometry analysis has significant limitations, with OpenEval providing comprehensive characterization and peer reviewers explicitly stating analyses erase valuable information and obscure results.
